passage: The storm knocked the power out just as Kiran sent her message: "Are you coming to study tomorrow?" She waited an hour, then two, staring at the dark screen. Nothing from Salma. Her mind started building stories. She's fed up with me. She found a better group. Kiran couldn't sleep, and the maths exam was at nine. At midnight she caught herself. She typed instead, "Hey, no pressure, but I'm worried I upset you. Are you okay?" She didn't expect an answer. In the morning it came: "So sorry! My phone died in the storm. See you at the library. Love you 😊"

qa.q: What knocked the power out?
qa.a: The storm knocked the power out.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while she waited for Salma's reply?
qa.a: She was anxious and worried she had upset Salma, and her imagination made up stories. The delay was actually because of a dead phone.

qa.q: What worked when Kiran finally asked?
qa.a: She sent a kind, direct message asking if Salma was okay instead of spiralling. Asking got a clear answer.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when she saw Kiran's message?
qa.a: She felt sorry and warm toward Kiran, as her reply shows. She had no idea her silence caused worry.

grounding: A teenager waits hours for a reply and imagines rejection, then asks directly and learns the delay was harmless.

passage: Harish had asked Ojas at ten if he'd join the cricket group. By four, no reply. Harish checked his phone over and over on the way home. He'd seen "read" and nothing else. Does he think I'm annoying? he wondered. He'd had a hard day and his mind ran on. In the flat lift he stopped himself and wrote, "No rush, but are you busy? Just checking you got that." Ten minutes later: "Sorry!! I've been helping mum at her shop all day. Yes! I'll be there. Thanks for asking." Harish laughed at his own worry and pocketed the phone.

qa.q: What did Harish ask Ojas at ten?
qa.a: He asked if Ojas would join the cricket group.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he checked his phone?
qa.a: He was anxious and worried that Ojas thought he was annoying. He had also had a hard day, which fed the worry.

qa.q: What could Harish do next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: Wait a bit, then send a friendly message asking if the person is busy. That is wiser than spiralling.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt when he saw Harish's check-in?
qa.a: He was probably apologetic and pleased to be included. He had simply been busy with his mother.

grounding: A teenager waits hours for a reply, imagines rejection, then asks directly and finds the person was busy.

passage:
"Francis, you didn't reply for six hours yesterday."
"I know, I know."
"I thought you were angry about the match. I kept checking my phone."
"Tenzin, my phone died at my grandmother's. She doesn't have a charger that fits."
"Six hours!"
"I'm sorry. Were you worried?"
"I was sure you were upset with me. I even typed a long apology."
"For what?"
"For the missed pass."
Francis laughed. "I forgot about the pass!"
Tenzin groaned. "I wasted my whole evening worrying."
"Next time just call me. Or ask straight away. Don't spiral."
"Okay. But charge your phone."
"Deal."

qa.q: Why didn't Francis reply for six hours?
qa.a: His phone died at his grandmother's.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Tenzin felt anxious and worried, sure that Francis was upset about the missed pass.

qa.q: What does Francis suggest for next time?
qa.a: Francis suggests calling or asking straight away instead of spiralling over a delayed reply.

qa.q: How did Francis see the delayed reply?
qa.a: Francis didn't think it meant anything, since his phone had died and he had forgotten the pass.

grounding: Two teenagers talk about a delayed text reply that was read as anger, and asking directly is wiser than spiralling.

passage:
Last year, after I told Pallavi that my parents were thinking of separating, she didn't reply for a whole day. I kept looking at the two ticks. I thought she didn't care. I thought maybe I'd said too much.
By evening I'd convinced myself she was avoiding me.
The next morning, I asked her straight out at the gate. "Why didn't you reply?"
She looked upset. "I didn't know what to say. I wrote five messages and deleted them all. I didn't want to say something stupid."
Then she hugged me.
I learned something that day. A slow reply doesn't always mean they don't care. Sometimes it means they care so much they're scared to get it wrong.
- Ankita

qa.q: How many messages did Pallavi write and delete?
qa.a: Five messages.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling while waiting for Pallavi's reply?
qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and hurt, thinking Pallavi didn't care or was avoiding the conversation.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that stopped the spiral?
qa.a: Ankita asked Pallavi directly the next morning, which revealed the real reason for the delay.

qa.q: How did Pallavi experience the delay?
qa.a: Pallavi was unsure what to say and worried about saying something wrong, so she delayed because she cared.

grounding: The narrator recalls reading a friend's delayed reply as rejection, and asking directly revealing she was unsure what to say.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday
Amandeep came to see me today, visibly upset. He said Binita had left his message on "seen" since Saturday. He was sure she was angry with him, and he'd barely slept.
I asked him what else could explain it. He thought for a while. "Maybe she's busy with her cousin's wedding? Or doesn't know how to reply?"
I suggested he ask her directly and kindly, instead of guessing.
He texted her from my office: "Hey, just checking we're okay?"
She replied in ten minutes: "Of course! Sorry, wedding chaos. Talk tonight?"
Amandeep laughed with relief. We talked about how often delays mean nothing bad.
- Ms Rodrigues, school counsellor

qa.q: Since when had Binita left the message on "seen"?
qa.a: Since Saturday.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: Amandeep felt anxious and upset, convinced Binita was angry and barely sleeping.

qa.q: What did Ms Rodrigues do that helped?
qa.a: She helped Amandeep consider other reasons and encouraged him to ask Binita directly and kindly.

qa.q: How did Binita see her own delayed reply?
qa.a: Binita didn't mean anything by it; she was busy with her cousin's wedding.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager spiralling over a delayed reply and asking directly revealing it was just busyness.

passage:
Tuesday night
Sent Chandrika the audition video at 4:10. Blue ticks at 4:12. Then NOTHING. By six I had decided she thought it was terrible and was too kind to say so. By seven I had re-watched it eleven times and found every flat note. Amma said, "Ganga, beti, the phone won't answer faster if you stare at it." At dinner I nearly typed "fine, forget it" but didn't. Instead I wrote: "hey, are you busy or did you hate it? either is ok, just tell me 🙂" Honestly only half ok. Reply at 9:40: "SORRY. Tuition till 9, phone in the bag. Watched it on the bus and wanted to write something proper, not just 'nice'. The high part gave me goosebumps!!" So: five hours of spiralling for a bus ride and tuition. Note to self: ask first, panic later.

qa.q: When did Chandrika's reply arrive?
qa.a: The reply arrived at 9:40.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Ganga felt anxious and afraid of rejection, deciding by six that Chandrika thought the video was terrible and re-watching it eleven times. Some of it may also have been nerves about the audition itself.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Ganga read the silence as a verdict and spiralled for hours; a direct, low-pressure question brought the real reason, tuition and a phone in the bag. 👍

qa.q: Why might Chandrika have waited to reply?
qa.a: Chandrika was at tuition till nine and then wanted to write something proper rather than just 'nice', so the delay came from care, not rejection.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a long reply delay as rejection, spiralling, and then asking directly and learning the delay meant something else.
